The section will explain how the integration of LLMs into complex, tool-using systems has rendered static heuristic defenses brittle, creating a landscape where adversaries and models co-evolve in real-time.

outline.description: Framing hallucinations as a critical security and reliability vulnerability, this section details the profound maturation in theoretical understanding and methodological sophistication between 2023 and 2025. It will contrast the early normative view of hallucinations as strict errors with more recent theoretical reframings. The narrative will begin with the foundational work of [Friel_2023_LLM], discussing the use of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting to elicit boolean judgments and human-readable justifications. It will then transition to the 2024 bifurcation of research into theoretical reframing and the engineering of scalable annotation systems, highlighting [Gu_2024_Anah]'s iterative approach to overcoming the prohibitive labor costs and unreliability of proprietary APIs like GPT-4 for fine-grained hallucination annotation.

outline.title: Cross-Cutting Defenses and Mitigation Strategies
outline.description: This section provides a holistic overview of defense mechanisms across the various threat categories, tracing the evolution from static to dynamic defenses. It will discuss the brittleness of early static prompt engineering, simple perplexity checks, and basic instruction filtering against modern attacks. Furthermore, it will explore the rise of dynamic, co-evolutionary defense mechanisms designed to counter automated adaptive attacks and Indirect Prompt Injections in agentic workflows, proposing a unified defense architecture for future LLM deployments.

outline.title: Discussion and Open Challenges
outline.description: This section critically analyzes the gaps, limitations, and future directions in LLM security research. It will address the escalating threat of multi-modal vulnerabilities and the challenges of securing autonomous, tool-using LLM agents against Indirect Prompt Injection. The discussion will emphasize the ongoing arms race between automated attack generation and dynamic defenses. Furthermore, it will highlight the critical open challenge of evaluation bottlenecks, specifically the over-reliance on proprietary, opaque APIs for benchmarking, and the urgent need for open, massive-scale, systemic benchmarking frameworks that can keep pace with rapid model evolution.

outline.title: Conclusion
outline.description: The conclusion synthesizes the core findings of the survey, reiterating the profound shift in the LLM security landscape from static, isolated vulnerabilities to dynamic, systemic, and agentic threats. It will provide actionable, practical recommendations for researchers and practitioners, emphasizing the necessity of integrating security at both the training (anti-poisoning) and inference (dynamic filtering, stateful detection) stages. The section will close with a forward-looking statement on the imperative of collaborative, open-source benchmarking to ensure the safe deployment of next-generation generative models.

introduction.title: Introduction
introduction.text:
# Introduction

## Motivation
The emergence of artificial intelligence has marked a significant transformation in Natural Language Processing (NLP) through the introduction of Large Language Models (LLMs), enabling unprecedented advances in language comprehension, generation, and translation [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. Models such as OpenAI's ChatGPT and GPT-4 have outperformed previous state-of-the-art methods across a wide variety of benchmarking tasks, demonstrating remarkable capabilities in reasoning, planning, and interacting with complex environments [Yang_2024_Adversarial]. These transformative impacts extend beyond general-purpose chatbots, holding significant potential in specialized, high-stakes domains such as healthcare, finance, and autonomous systems. 

However, with their rising prominence and integration into critical infrastructure, the security and vulnerability aspects of these models have garnered significant attention [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. The very capabilities that make LLMs powerful—their ability to process vast amounts of unstructured data and generate contextually relevant responses—also render them susceptible to a novel class of security threats. For instance, the persistent challenge of hallucinations, where models generate inaccurate or unmotivated claims, undermines their reliability and trustworthiness [Friel_2023_LLM]. Beyond unintentional errors, malicious actors can exploit LLMs through sophisticated adversarial techniques. Generative LLMs have been shown to be vulnerable to backdoor attacks, where carefully crafted triggers in the input manipulate the model to produce adversary-specified outputs [Li_2024_Backdoorllm]. Furthermore, as LLMs evolve into autonomous agents capable of using external tools, they become exposed to indirect prompt injection attacks, a critical security risk that can compromise the entire agentic ecosystem [Wang_2025_LLM]. The rapid proliferation of these threats necessitates a comprehensive understanding of the LLM security landscape, motivating this survey to systematically analyze the vulnerabilities, attack vectors, and defense mechanisms associated with modern language models.

## Scope of Survey
This survey provides a comprehensive and structured overview of the security and privacy vulnerabilities inherent in Large Language Models, alongside an in-depth analysis of state-of-the-art defense strategies. The scope of this paper is deliberately focused on vulnerabilities that are unique to the architecture, training methodologies, and deployment paradigms of LLMs, rather than traditional software or network security issues. 

Specifically, our investigation encompasses four primary domains of LLM security. First, we explore **Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking**, detailing how malicious inputs can bypass safety guardrails. This includes both direct prompt injections and the increasingly prevalent indirect prompt injections (IPI) that target LLM agents interacting with external environments [Zhan_2025_LLM, Wang_2025_LLM]. We also review automated defense strategies, such as prompt-based detection frameworks [Liu_2025_Aegis]. Second, we examine **Data and Model Poisoning**, focusing on how adversaries can compromise the training or fine-tuning phases. This covers lightweight knowledge editing for backdoor injection [Li_2024_Badedit] and the manipulation of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) mechanisms [Duan_2025_RLHF]. Third, we address **Adversarial Attacks**, particularly in specialized domains where the robustness of LLMs is critical [Yang_2024_Adversarial]. Finally, we analyze the phenomenon of **LLM Hallucinations**, treating it not merely as a performance artifact but as a fundamental reliability and security concern that requires automated detection metrics [Friel_2023_LLM]. 

While this survey touches upon the intersection of LLMs with multimodal systems (e.g., text-to-image models) [Duan_2025_RLHF], the primary emphasis remains on text-based generative models and agentic frameworks. We do not cover hardware-level vulnerabilities or traditional denial-of-service attacks, ensuring a concentrated focus on the algorithmic and data-driven vulnerabilities of LLMs.

## Temporal Trends (2023-2026)
The landscape of LLM security has evolved at a breakneck pace, reflecting the rapid advancements in the underlying technologies. By analyzing the literature from 2023 to the projected trends of 2026, we observe a distinct trajectory from the discovery of foundational vulnerabilities to the emergence of complex, agent-based threats.

**2023: The Year of Discovery and Reliability.** In 2023, as LLMs gained mainstream adoption, the research community primarily focused on understanding their fundamental limitations. A major theme was the identification and measurement of hallucinations, driven by the need to ensure coherent and factually accurate outputs [Friel_2023_LLM]. Early forms of prompt injection and basic jailbreaks were also documented, prompting the initial wave of heuristic defenses and safety alignment techniques.

**2024: Sophistication in Poisoning and Adversarial Tactics.** By 2024, the focus shifted towards more sophisticated, stealthy attacks targeting the model's weights and training pipeline. Researchers demonstrated that LLMs were highly susceptible to data and model poisoning, introducing backdoor attacks that required minimal tuning data [Li_2024_Backdoorllm, Li_2024_Badedit]. Furthermore, the application of LLMs in critical sectors like healthcare highlighted the severe implications of adversarial attacks, pushing the community to develop domain-specific robustness evaluations [Yang_2024_Adversarial, Chowdhury_2024_Breaking].

**2025: The Era of Agentic Vulnerabilities and Automated Defenses.** The current year, 2025, is characterized by the widespread deployment of LLM agents capable of tool use and environmental interaction. This paradigm shift has introduced severe risks, notably indirect prompt injections, where malicious instructions are embedded in external data sources accessed by the agent [Zhan_2025_LLM]. In response, sophisticated fuzzing frameworks like AGENTVIGIL have been developed to systematically evaluate these black-box agents [Wang_2025_LLM]. Concurrently, defenses have become more automated and adaptive, moving away from manual prompt engineering towards autonomous generation of detection prompts [Liu_2025_Aegis]. Additionally, vulnerabilities in alignment techniques, such as the hijacking of RLHF mechanisms, have become a critical area of study [Duan_2025_RLHF].

**2026 (Projected): Autonomous Ecosystems and Certified Robustness.** Looking ahead to 2026, we anticipate the emergence of autonomous attack-defense ecosystems, where AI systems continuously probe and patch vulnerabilities in real-time. As regulatory frameworks around AI safety mature, there will likely be a strong push towards certified robustness, requiring mathematical guarantees of an LLM's resilience against specific classes of attacks.

## Contributions
In light of the rapidly shifting threat landscape, this survey aims to consolidate fragmented research into a cohesive framework, providing a foundational resource for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers. The primary contributions of this paper are manifold:

1. **Systematic Taxonomy of LLM Vulnerabilities:** We propose a novel, comprehensive taxonomy that categorizes LLM security threats based on the attack surface (e.g., inference-time vs. training-time), the adversary's capabilities, and the targeted component of the LLM pipeline. This structured approach facilitates a clearer understanding of the diverse threat vectors, from hallucinations [Friel_2023_LLM] to complex backdoor injections [Li_2024_Badedit].

2. **In-depth Analysis of Agentic Security:** Recognizing the paradigm shift towards autonomous systems, we provide one of the first extensive reviews dedicated to the security of LLM agents. We critically examine the mechanics of indirect prompt injection attacks [Wang_2025_LLM, Zhan_2025_LLM] and evaluate the efficacy of current defense mechanisms in dynamic, tool-use environments.

3. **Evaluation of State-of-the-Art Defenses:** We systematically review and compare recent defense strategies, highlighting the transition from static, manual guardrails to dynamic, automated defense frameworks [Liu_2025_Aegis]. We also assess the robustness of alignment techniques like RLHF against adversarial manipulation [Duan_2025_RLHF].

4. **Temporal Mapping and Future Directions:** By mapping the evolution of attacks and defenses from 2023 to 2026, we identify critical gaps in the current literature. We outline strategic future research directions, emphasizing the need for scalable, certified defenses and robust evaluation metrics tailored for high-stakes domains [Yang_2024_Adversarial].

Through these contributions, this survey not only illuminates the current state of LLM security but also charts a course for developing resilient, trustworthy artificial intelligence systems capable of withstanding the sophisticated threats of tomorrow.

# Background and Preliminaries

The rapid proliferation and integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into diverse applications have fundamentally transformed the landscape of Natural Language Processing (NLP) and artificial intelligence. These models offer unprecedented capabilities in language comprehension, generation, reasoning, and translation [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. However, as their deployment scales across critical sectors—ranging from healthcare automation to financial analysis and autonomous agents—the security and vulnerability aspects of these systems have garnered significant attention [Yang_2024_Adversarial]. Understanding the foundational mechanics of LLMs, alongside the multifaceted threats they face, is essential for developing robust mitigation strategies. This section provides the necessary background and preliminaries, detailing the basics of LLM architecture, establishing a comprehensive threat taxonomy, defining attacker capabilities, and distinguishing between black-box and white-box attack paradigms.

## LLM Architecture Basics

To comprehend the vulnerabilities inherent in Large Language Models, it is first necessary to understand their underlying architectural framework. Modern LLMs are predominantly built upon the Transformer architecture, a deep learning model introduced to handle sequential data efficiently through massive parallelization. Unlike earlier recurrent neural networks (RNNs) that process data sequentially, Transformers rely entirely on self-attention mechanisms to draw global dependencies between input and output tokens.

**The Transformer and Self-Attention Mechanism:**
At the core of the Transformer architecture is the self-attention mechanism, which allows the model to weigh the importance of different words (or tokens) in a sequence relative to a specific target word, regardless of their positional distance. This mechanism enables LLMs to capture complex contextual relationships and long-range dependencies within text. The attention mechanism computes a weighted sum of values, where the weight assigned to each value is determined by the compatibility of a query with the corresponding key. Recent research has explored utilizing these attention contributions to categorize input queries and detect model hallucinations, highlighting the critical role attention plays in determining model outputs [Liu_2025_Attention]. However, this same mechanism can be exploited by adversaries who craft inputs specifically designed to manipulate attention weights, forcing the model to focus on malicious instructions while ignoring safety guardrails.

**Pre-training and Fine-tuning:**
The development of an LLM typically follows a two-stage process: pre-training and fine-tuning. During the pre-training phase, the model is exposed to massive, diverse corpora of text data scraped from the internet. The objective is usually self-supervised, such as predicting the next token in a sequence (causal language modeling). This phase endows the model with a broad understanding of grammar, facts, reasoning abilities, and, inadvertently, the biases and toxicities present in the training data.

Following pre-training, the model undergoes fine-tuning to align its outputs with specific tasks or human preferences. This often involves instruction tuning, where the model is trained on datasets of instruction-response pairs, and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), which optimizes the model to generate responses that human evaluators deem helpful and safe. While these processes refine the model's capabilities, they also introduce distinct attack vectors. For instance, individuals and organizations frequently download pre-trained LLMs from open-source repositories (e.g., HuggingFace) for subsequent tuning and deployment, creating opportunities for adversaries to introduce vulnerabilities during the specialized tuning phase [Li_2024_Badedit].

**Explainability and Vulnerability:**
The sheer scale of these models—often comprising billions or hundreds of billions of parameters—renders them highly opaque. The explainability of LLMs is pivotal not just for enhancing transparency and trustworthiness, but also for identifying and mitigating vulnerabilities to linguistic attacks [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. The complex, non-linear decision-making processes inherent within the deep layers of the Transformer make it challenging to predict exactly how a model will respond to adversarial or edge-case inputs, necessitating a structured approach to understanding potential threats.

## Threat Taxonomy

As LLMs become integral to automated systems and decision-making processes, they are exposed to a diverse range of threats. Categorizing the LLM attacks literature into a structured taxonomy is crucial for understanding the landscape of vulnerabilities and aiding future defensive research [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. The threat taxonomy for LLMs can be broadly classified into several key areas based on the attack vector and the lifecycle stage at which the attack occurs.

**1. Data and Model Poisoning:**
Poisoning attacks occur during the training or fine-tuning phases of the LLM lifecycle. Adversaries inject malicious data into the training corpus to manipulate the model's behavior systematically. This can result in the model learning incorrect associations, adopting specific biases, or embedding hidden backdoors that can be triggered later by specific input patterns. Because LLMs require vast amounts of data, ensuring the absolute purity of the training set is practically impossible, making poisoning a persistent and stealthy threat [Li_2024_Backdoorllm].

**2. Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking:**
Prompt injection attacks target the inference phase, where the model is actively processing user inputs. In these attacks, adversaries craft malicious inputs designed to override the model's original system instructions or safety guardrails. Direct prompt injection involves the user inputting the malicious command directly into the chat interface. Conversely, Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) occurs when an LLM agent processes external data (e.g., reading a webpage, summarizing a document, or interacting with an API) that contains hidden malicious instructions. Despite defenses designed for IPI attacks, their robustness remains questionable due to the evolving nature of these exploits [Zhan_2025_LLM]. Jailbreaking is a specific sub-category of prompt injection aimed at bypassing ethical and safety filters to elicit restricted, illegal, or harmful content.

**3. Adversarial Attacks:**
Adversarial attacks involve introducing subtle, often human-imperceptible perturbations to the input text that cause the model to make errors, misclassify intents, or behave unexpectedly. These attacks range from human-crafted, non-scalable methods to automated techniques utilizing search algorithms, target function optimization, and even other LLMs to generate adversarial examples [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking].

**4. Information Extraction and Privacy Leaks:**
These threats focus on forcing the LLM to regurgitate sensitive, confidential, or personally identifiable information (PII) that it may have memorized during its pre-training phase. Attackers use carefully constructed prompts to probe the model's memory, exploiting the model's tendency to reproduce its training data under certain prompting conditions.

## Attacker Capabilities

To accurately assess the risk posed by the threats outlined in the taxonomy, it is essential to define the capabilities of potential attackers. The threat model dictates what an adversary can and cannot do, which in turn influences the types of attacks they can execute and the defenses required to thwart them. Attacker capabilities in the context of LLM security can be delineated across several dimensions.

**Lifecycle Access:**
An attacker's capability is heavily dependent on which stage of the LLM lifecycle they can access. 
- *Training Phase Capabilities:* Attackers with access to the training pipeline can execute broad and devastating threat models. They may be capable of manipulating training data (data poisoning), modifying model parameters directly (weight poisoning), influencing the training process, or manipulating hidden states [Li_2024_Backdoorllm]. This level of access is highly privileged but can occur in scenarios involving compromised supply chains, malicious insiders, or the reliance on untrusted third-party datasets.
- *Deployment/Inference Phase Capabilities:* Most attackers operate at this stage. They interact with the deployed model as a standard user or through an API. Their capabilities are generally restricted to crafting inputs (prompts) and observing outputs, though they may leverage zero-shot or few-shot inference techniques to manipulate the model's context window [Li_2024_Badedit].

**Specific Threat Models and Sophistication:**
Recent literature explicitly distinguishes between different threat models based on the attacker's role and interaction with the system. For example, in LLM-as-a-judge scenarios, a "Content-Author Attack" model is defined. In this scenario, a malicious content author submits text for evaluation that contains adversarial elements specifically designed to manipulate the LLM judge's assessment. The submitted text passes through the evaluation pipeline unchanged, representing a realistic capability where the attacker controls the data being processed but not the processing system itself [Maloyan_2025_LLM].

Furthermore, attackers possess varying levels of computational resources and sophistication. Some may rely on manual, human-crafted prompts, which are slow and non-scalable. In contrast, well-resourced attackers might employ automated methods, utilizing optimization algorithms or leveraging other LLMs to generate sophisticated, high-volume attacks [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. The capability to hijack advanced reasoning processes, such as Chain-of-Thought (CoT) hijacking, demonstrates a high level of sophistication where the attacker manipulates the intermediate reasoning steps of the model to force a desired, often malicious, final output [Li_2024_Backdoorllm].

## Black-box vs. White-box Attacks

A fundamental distinction in the evaluation of LLM vulnerabilities is the classification of attacks based on the adversary's knowledge of and access to the target model. This dichotomy—black-box versus white-box—defines the strategies available to the attacker and the complexity of the required defenses.

**White-box Attacks:**
White-box attacks assume that the adversary has complete, transparent access to the target LLM. This includes full knowledge of the model's architecture, the underlying algorithms, the training data, the hyper-parameters, and, crucially, the model's internal weights and gradients. 

This level of access permits highly sophisticated and targeted exploits. Attackers can utilize gradient-based optimization techniques to craft adversarial inputs that are mathematically guaranteed to alter outputs, impair performance, or extract sensitive information [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. Because the attacker can compute the exact gradient of the loss function with respect to the input, they can systematically perturb the input tokens to maximize the probability of a malicious outcome. While white-box scenarios represent the most powerful attacker capability, they are often less realistic for proprietary, closed-source models (e.g., OpenAI's GPT-4 or Anthropic's Claude), where the internal mechanics are strictly guarded. However, with the proliferation of powerful open-source models (e.g., Meta's LLaMA series), white-box threat models have become highly relevant, as adversaries can download and analyze these models locally.

**Black-box Attacks:**
In contrast, black-box attacks operate under the assumption that the adversary has limited or no knowledge of the model's internal workings. The attacker interacts with the LLM solely through its input-output interface, typically via an API or a user chat interface. They do not have access to the model's architecture, weights, or gradients.

Black-box attacks focus on manipulating or degrading performance by observing how the model responds to various inputs. This approach is highly realistic in practical, real-world scenarios, especially when targeting commercial, proprietary LLMs [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. Attackers in a black-box setting often rely on heuristic methods, trial-and-error, or transferability—where an adversarial example crafted on a known, open-source surrogate model (a white-box environment) is deployed against the unknown target model with the expectation that the vulnerability transfers across architectures. 

Despite the lack of internal access, black-box attacks pose severe risks, including sensitive data extraction, the generation of biased or harmful outputs, and the execution of prompt injection and jailbreaking techniques. The success of black-box attacks highlights that securing the model's weights is insufficient; the input-output interface itself represents a significant attack surface that must be rigorously defended to maintain trust and reliability in AI systems [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking].

**Model Reliability and Trust: LLM Hallucinations**

**Introduction to LLM Hallucinations**
Large Language Models (LLMs) have witnessed significant advancements in recent years, demonstrating remarkable capabilities in generating coherent, intelligent, and contextually relevant responses across a wide array of tasks and domains. From creative writing and coding to complex problem-solving and long-form question answering, these models have become ubiquitous in both academic research and commercial applications. However, despite their impressive fluency and apparent reasoning abilities, LLMs are plagued by a persistent and critical challenge: hallucinations. In the context of natural language processing, hallucinations—often referred to as confabulations—occur when a model generates information that is factually incorrect, nonsensical, or unfaithful to the provided source material or established world knowledge. 

Hallucination has emerged as a significant barrier to the effective application and widespread adoption of LLMs in high-stakes environments [Liu_2025_Attention]. When models produce plausible-sounding but inaccurate claims, they undermine user trust and pose substantial risks in domains such as healthcare, legal advising, and financial forecasting, where precision and factual correctness are paramount. The presence of these inaccurate or unmotivated claims necessitates the development of robust, automated metrics and methodologies for the detection and mitigation of hallucinations in LLM outputs [Friel_2023_LLM]. As artificial intelligence rapidly integrates into science, scholarship, and daily life, addressing the hallucination problem is widely viewed as a critical bottleneck that must be overcome to ensure model reliability and foster user trust [Sui_2024_Confabulation].

**Theoretical Reframing of Hallucinations**
Historically, the integration of LLMs into natural language processing discourse has been accompanied by a predominantly negative view of hallucinations. The standard perspective posits that confabulations are inherently problematic—a conspicuous social harm and a fundamental flaw that AI research must strive to eliminate entirely [Sui_2024_Confabulation]. Under this paradigm, hallucinations are treated as bugs or errors in the model's generation process, stemming from issues such as training data memorization, flawed probabilistic sampling, or an inability to ground generated text in verifiable facts. Consequently, the primary objective of much of the research in this area has been to suppress these outputs through techniques like reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and rigorous fact-checking pipelines.

However, recent scholarship has proposed a compelling theoretical reframing of this phenomenon. Rather than viewing hallucinations exclusively as a categorically negative pitfall, some researchers argue for a systematic defense of LLM confabulations, suggesting they can be understood and even leveraged as a potential resource [Sui_2024_Confabulation]. This alternative framework challenges the binary classification of model outputs as strictly "true" or "false," recognizing that the generative nature of LLMs—which allows them to synthesize novel combinations of concepts—is the very same mechanism that produces hallucinations. 

When an LLM generates a novel story, writes poetry, or brainstorms solutions to a complex problem, it is essentially confabulating—drawing connections between disparate concepts in its training data to produce something entirely new. If we strictly penalize any deviation from established facts, we risk stifling the model's creative potential. Therefore, the theoretical reframing advocates for a context-aware evaluation paradigm. In domains requiring strict adherence to facts, such as medical diagnosis or legal precedent analysis, hallucinations remain a critical flaw. However, in creative or exploratory domains, these same confabulations can serve as a powerful engine for innovation. Embracing this perspective allows the AI community to move beyond a purely adversarial relationship with hallucinations, fostering a more comprehensive understanding of generative language models.

**Detection and Mitigation Strategies: The Role of Chain-of-Thought (CoT)**
To build trust in LLMs, it is essential to develop effective strategies for detecting and mitigating hallucinations when factual accuracy is required. One of the most promising avenues of research involves leveraging the models' own reasoning capabilities through advanced prompting techniques, such as Chain-of-Thought (CoT). CoT prompting encourages the model to articulate its intermediate reasoning steps before arriving at a final answer, thereby making its internal logic more transparent and easier to verify. By forcing the model to externalize its thought process, developers can pinpoint exactly where a hallucination originates—whether it is a failure in retrieving the correct premise, a logical fallacy in the intermediate steps, or a flawed conclusion drawn from accurate premises. This granularity is invaluable for debugging and refining model architectures.

A notable advancement in this area is the development of automated metrics that utilize polling and reasoning to assess model outputs. For instance, the ChainPoll approach represents a state-of-the-art method for hallucination detection [Friel_2023_LLM]. ChainPoll operates by prompting a powerful LLM (such as GPT-3.5-Turbo) to evaluate whether a given completion contains hallucinations. This is achieved using a detailed, carefully engineered prompt that guides the evaluator model through a reasoning process. Crucially, ChainPoll runs this evaluation multiple times—typically five—using batch inference for speed, and aggregates the results to form a consensus [Friel_2023_LLM]. By combining the structured reasoning of CoT-like prompts with the statistical robustness of polling, ChainPoll significantly outperforms other detection methods, such as SelfCheck-BertScore, across a diverse range of benchmark tasks, offering a highly efficient and accurate metric for identifying inaccurate claims [Friel_2023_LLM].

In addition to polling methods, researchers are exploring zero-shot hallucination detection techniques that do not rely on external knowledge bases or extensive fine-tuning. The Attention-Guided SElf-Reflection (AGSER) approach is one such novel method [Liu_2025_Attention]. AGSER utilizes the model's internal attention contributions to categorize the input query into attentive and non-attentive segments. By analyzing how the model allocates its attention during the generation process, AGSER can trigger self-reflection mechanisms that help the model identify and correct potential hallucinations on the fly [Liu_2025_Attention]. These introspective techniques, which capitalize on the model's architectural features and reasoning pathways, represent a critical step toward creating self-correcting LLMs that can autonomously maintain high standards of reliability.

**Scalable Annotation for Hallucination Detection**
While automated detection metrics like ChainPoll and AGSER are vital, their development and evaluation rely heavily on high-quality datasets. Creating comprehensive datasets for hallucination detection and mitigation is a formidable challenge, particularly in long-form question-answering tasks that span various domains [Gu_2024_Anah]. Current datasets are often limited in both domain coverage and size, which restricts their utility in training robust, generalizable detection models. The primary bottleneck in expanding these datasets is the prohibitive labor cost associated with human annotation. Evaluating long-form, complex model responses for subtle factual inaccuracies requires significant time, domain expertise, and cognitive effort from human annotators.

To overcome these limitations, the research community is increasingly focusing on scalable annotation strategies. The goal is to develop automated or semi-automated pipelines that can generate large-scale, high-quality hallucination annotations without relying exclusively on expensive human labor. One effective approach involves a progressive scaling strategy designed to stabilize and enhance the performance of automated annotators [Gu_2024_Anah]. In this framework, the annotation process is broken down into stages. Initially, a robust annotator model is developed and calibrated on a smaller, well-defined set of topics. Once the annotator demonstrates sufficient accuracy and reliability, the dataset is progressively expanded to include a wider number of topics and questions [Gu_2024_Anah]. 

This progressive scaling allows the automated annotator to adapt to unfamiliar responses across diverse subjects, ensuring that the quality of the annotations remains consistent as the dataset grows [Gu_2024_Anah]. By leveraging powerful LLMs to annotate the outputs of other models, researchers can rapidly construct large-scale datasets that capture a wide variety of hallucination types. These scalable annotation frameworks are essential for training the next generation of hallucination detectors, providing the volume and diversity of data needed to capture the nuanced ways in which LLMs confabulate information.

**Ensuring Reliability in LLM Outputs and Annotators**
The push towards scalable, automated annotation introduces a secondary, yet equally critical, challenge: ensuring the reliability of the automated annotators themselves. When relying on LLMs to detect hallucinations in other LLMs, there is an inherent risk of compounding errors. Due to the insufficiency of accurate human annotations for large-scale validation, the reliability of existing hallucination annotators and detectors has become a pressing concern within the AI community [Gu_2024_Anah]. 

Studies have shown that even the most powerful and sophisticated LLMs, such as GPT-4, are not infallible when acting as evaluators. These models can produce inaccurate results, misclassifying correct information as hallucinations or failing to identify subtle factual errors [Gu_2024_Anah]. This unreliability stems from the same fundamental limitations that cause hallucinations in the first place: the models lack true grounding in external reality and can be swayed by plausible-sounding but incorrect reasoning. When an automated annotator evaluates a response sentence by sentence, it may struggle to maintain global context or verify highly specialized domain knowledge, leading to inconsistent or erroneous annotations [Gu_2024_Anah].

To build genuine trust in LLM applications, it is imperative to address the reliability of both the generative models and the systems used to evaluate them. This requires the development of multi-tiered evaluation frameworks that do not rely on a single point of failure. Techniques such as ensemble evaluation, where multiple diverse models assess an output and vote on its factual accuracy, can help mitigate the biases and blind spots of individual annotators. Furthermore, integrating external knowledge retrieval systems into the annotation pipeline can provide the automated evaluators with verifiable facts, grounding their assessments in reliable source material.

Ultimately, achieving model reliability and trust necessitates a holistic approach. It requires acknowledging the theoretical complexities of hallucinations—understanding them not just as errors, but as intrinsic features of generative models that must be managed [Sui_2024_Confabulation]. It demands the continuous refinement of detection methodologies, leveraging techniques like Chain-of-Thought reasoning and attention-guided reflection to enhance model transparency [Friel_2023_LLM, Liu_2025_Attention]. It also calls for innovative, scalable annotation strategies that can generate the vast datasets needed for training, while rigorously interrogating the reliability of the automated systems tasked with evaluating model performance [Gu_2024_Anah]. By addressing these interconnected challenges, the AI community can pave the way for LLMs that are not only highly capable but also consistently reliable and trustworthy in their real-world applications.

cross_cutting_defenses.title: Cross-Cutting Defenses and Mitigation Strategies
cross_cutting_defenses.text:
**Cross-Cutting Defenses and Mitigation Strategies**

As the deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) and advanced machine learning systems becomes increasingly ubiquitous, the threat landscape surrounding these technologies has grown exponentially in complexity and sophistication. Adversaries continuously develop novel techniques to exploit vulnerabilities, ranging from data poisoning and backdoor injections to sophisticated prompt injection and query-based black-box attacks. Consequently, the security paradigm must shift from isolated, static countermeasures to comprehensive, cross-cutting defenses and mitigation strategies. This section explores the forefront of defensive research, detailing the mechanisms that aim to secure AI systems against a diverse array of adversarial threats. We delve into the critical roles of Dynamic Defenses, Adversarial Contrastive Prompt Tuning, Stateful Detection, Co-evolutionary Mechanisms, and overarching Mitigation Strategies, highlighting how these approaches interlock to create robust, resilient AI architectures.

**Dynamic Defenses**

The adversarial landscape is fundamentally characterized by an ongoing, relentless arms race. As defenders implement new security measures, attackers continually evolve their strategies to bypass them, necessitating a departure from static defense paradigms [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. Dynamic defenses represent a critical evolution in AI security, designed to adapt to shifting task demands and the fluid nature of adversarial settings. Unlike traditional defenses that rely on fixed rules or static models, dynamic defenses continuously update their parameters, strategies, or ensemble configurations in response to the operational environment and emerging threat vectors [Liu_2025_Aegis].

One of the primary motivations for dynamic defenses is the realization that performance on standard safety benchmarks does not necessarily equate to comprehensive robustness. For instance, an LLM's ability to successfully refuse harmful prompts during standard testing may provide a false sense of security, as it does not guarantee resilience against sophisticated, multi-turn jailbreaking attacks or novel adversarial inputs [Li_2024_Backdoorllm]. Therefore, robust defenses require task-aware mitigation strategies that dynamically adjust based on the specific context and the spectrum of attack types encountered in real-world deployments.

Furthermore, dynamic defenses are particularly suited for evolving task environments where both the objectives of the AI system and the nature of the threats may change over time. This direction, while complex due to the challenges of modeling dynamic behaviors, is essential for long-term security [Liu_2025_Aegis]. Techniques such as Robust Prompt Optimization (RPO) exemplify this approach by continuously refining system prompts to withstand adversarial pressure. Additionally, in the realm of adversarial transferability, dynamic ensemble frameworks have shown significant promise. By employing dynamic ensemble weighting strategies and feature optimal alignment, defenders can enhance the robustness of models against attacks that attempt to transfer adversarial examples across different architectures [Jia_2025_Adversarial]. Ultimately, dynamic defenses acknowledge that security is not a state to be achieved, but a continuous process of adaptation and vigilance.

**Adversarial Contrastive Prompt Tuning**

A significant challenge in defending against adversarial attacks, particularly in vision-language models and image encoders, is the development of robust feature extractors capable of distinguishing between benign inputs and subtle adversarial perturbations. Adversarial Contrastive Prompt Tuning (ACPT) emerges as a highly effective, state-of-the-art methodology to address this challenge [Wang_2024_Advqdet]. ACPT leverages the principles of contrastive learning, a self-supervised representation learning technique that trains powerful feature extractors by pulling together representations of similar samples while pushing apart dissimilar ones.

ACPT innovates upon standard contrastive learning by adopting a sophisticated two-stream prompt tuning paradigm: a clean stream and an adversarial stream [Wang_2024_Advqdet]. In the clean stream, the framework processes augmented views of a clean image, forming Clean-to-Clean (C2C) pairs. The primary objective of this stream is to pull together the augmented versions of the same clean image, ensuring that the model learns invariant and robust features under standard data augmentations. This establishes a strong baseline of feature representation.

The adversarial stream, however, is where ACPT truly distinguishes itself. This stream introduces adversarial examples into the contrastive learning process. It utilizes contrastive losses to pull together the representations of a clean image and all of its adversarial counterparts generated under various data augmentations [Wang_2024_Advqdet]. By forcing the model to map adversarial examples to the same feature space as their clean originals, ACPT effectively neutralizes the impact of the adversarial perturbations. Furthermore, the framework incorporates specific adversarial losses to enhance its robustness against adaptive attacks, where the adversary possesses knowledge of the defense mechanism.

The efficacy of ACPT is notable not only in its defensive capabilities but also in its efficiency and generalization. Even when finetuned exclusively on standard datasets like ImageNet, ACPT demonstrates superb zero-shot capability, meaning it can effectively detect adversarial examples across a wide range of unseen domains and datasets without requiring domain-specific retraining [Wang_2024_Advqdet]. This cross-domain robustness makes ACPT a highly versatile and powerful tool in the arsenal of cross-cutting defenses, particularly when integrated into broader detection frameworks.

**Stateful Detection**

While techniques like ACPT focus on robust feature representation, Stateful Detection addresses the behavioral patterns of adversaries, specifically targeting query-based black-box attacks. In a query-based threat model, the adversary does not have direct access to the target model's internal parameters or gradients. Instead, they must generate adversarial examples by iteratively making multiple queries to the target model and utilizing the model's output (e.g., confidence scores or hard labels) to optimize the adversarial perturbations [Wang_2024_Advqdet]. 

Stateful detection frameworks are motivated by the critical observation that these iterative optimization processes inherently require the attacker to submit a sequence of visually or semantically similar queries to the target model. A stateful defense mechanism capitalizes on this behavioral footprint by maintaining a history or "state" of past queries. For any current query submitted to the system, the stateful detection task is to determine whether there exists a historical query within the system's memory such that the similarity between the current and historical query exceeds a predefined threshold [Wang_2024_Advqdet]. If this threshold is breached, the system flags the sequence of queries as a potential attack.

Previous iterations of stateful detection, such as Blacklight, utilized techniques like hashing to compute distances between queries, proving robust against certain types of attacks, including Sybil attacks where an adversary uses multiple accounts to distribute queries. However, these early methods often suffered from a poor tradeoff between the detection rate and the false positive rate, occasionally flagging benign users who submitted similar queries [Wang_2024_Advqdet]. 

Modern stateful detection frameworks overcome these limitations by integrating highly robust feature extractors, such as those trained via Adversarial Contrastive Prompt Tuning (ACPT). By using an adversarially finetuned encoder to compute the similarity scores, the stateful detector becomes highly sensitive to the specific types of perturbations introduced by query-based attacks, while remaining invariant to benign similarities. This synergy between robust feature extraction and behavioral tracking exemplifies the power of cross-cutting defenses, providing a formidable barrier against adversaries attempting to probe and exploit black-box models [Wang_2024_Advqdet].

**Co-evolutionary Mechanisms**

To truly anticipate and mitigate the evolving strategies of adversaries, defense mechanisms must simulate the adversarial arms race during their development phase. Co-evolutionary mechanisms provide a structured, dynamic framework for achieving this, fostering the simultaneous and competitive development of both attack and defense strategies [Liu_2025_Aegis]. This approach is particularly relevant in the context of prompt injection attacks against LLMs, where the boundary between benign instructions and malicious payloads is often blurred.

Within a co-evolutionary framework, the system is typically divided into two competing modules: an attacker module and a defender module. The attacker module's objective is to generate sophisticated adversarial prompts that can be injected into the original system prompt, aiming to mislead the LLM into executing unauthorized actions or bypassing safety filters. Conversely, the defender module aims to develop robust system prompts that can withstand these adversarial injections while simultaneously maintaining high utility and accuracy on benign inputs [Liu_2025_Aegis].

The core of the co-evolutionary mechanism lies in its alternating turns of evolution. The attacker evolves against a fixed version of the defender, striving to find vulnerabilities in the current defensive posture. Once the attacker has optimized its adversarial prompts, these prompts are fixed, and the defender evolves in response, learning to neutralize the newly discovered attack vectors [Liu_2025_Aegis]. This iterative process simulates a real-world arms race, pushing both modules to their limits.

This competitive dynamic consistently improves both attack and defense capabilities over successive iterations. By continuously exposing the defender to increasingly sophisticated and diverse attacks generated by the co-evolving attacker, the system achieves state-of-the-art robustness against real-world injection attempts [Liu_2025_Aegis]. Furthermore, advanced co-evolutionary frameworks often incorporate techniques like gradient replay to prevent catastrophic forgetting, ensuring that the defender retains its robustness against earlier attack strategies while adapting to new ones. Ablation studies have confirmed that this combination of co-evolution and memory retention is critical for sustaining long-term robustness in highly dynamic threat environments [Liu_2025_Aegis].

**Mitigation Strategies**

The culmination of dynamic defenses, robust feature extraction, behavioral tracking, and co-evolutionary training forms the foundation of comprehensive mitigation strategies. Mitigation strategies for protecting LLMs and AI systems can be broadly divided into distinct categories based on their deployment strategy, such as pre-deployment hardening (e.g., adversarial training, robust prompt optimization) and post-deployment monitoring (e.g., stateful detection, input filtering) [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking].

A critical aspect of effective mitigation is the recognition that no single defense is impenetrable. Developing defenses against adversarial attacks requires addressing not only existing, known attack vectors but also anticipating future, unforeseen threats [Zhan_2025_LLM]. Research has consistently demonstrated that adaptive attacks—where the adversary possesses knowledge of the specific defense mechanism in place—can frequently bypass isolated security measures. For instance, adaptive attacks have been shown to successfully break various defenses designed against indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks on LLM agents, highlighting the fragility of static defensive postures [Zhan_2025_LLM].

Therefore, robust mitigation strategies must employ a defense-in-depth approach, layering multiple cross-cutting mechanisms to create overlapping fields of security. By combining the proactive resilience generated by co-evolutionary mechanisms [Liu_2025_Aegis] and Adversarial Contrastive Prompt Tuning [Wang_2024_Advqdet] with the reactive, behavioral monitoring of Stateful Detection [Wang_2024_Advqdet], organizations can significantly elevate the cost and complexity for attackers. Ultimately, effective mitigation is an ongoing commitment to continuous research, dynamic adaptation, and the holistic integration of diverse security paradigms to safeguard the integrity and reliability of advanced AI systems [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking].

discussion_and_open_challenges.title: Discussion and Open Challenges
discussion_and_open_challenges.text:
**Discussion and Open Challenges**

The rapid advancement and widespread deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) and their multimodal extensions have ushered in transformative capabilities across diverse domains. However, as these models become increasingly integrated into critical applications, their security vulnerabilities have surfaced as a paramount concern. While significant progress has been made in identifying threats such as jailbreaks, prompt injections, and data poisoning, defense mechanisms often lag behind the sophisticated and evolving nature of these attacks. This section delves into the open challenges that persist in the field, highlighting specific areas such as multi-modal threats, evaluation bottlenecks, and agentic security, before charting potential future directions for research and development.

**Open Challenges**

The current landscape of LLM security is characterized by a continuous arms race between adversaries and defenders. One of the primary open challenges is the inherent tension between model utility and safety. Efforts to align models and implement robust guardrails frequently result in the degradation of the model's performance on benign tasks, leading to a phenomenon known as the "alignment tax." Furthermore, the black-box nature of many state-of-the-art commercial models obscures their internal mechanisms, making it difficult for researchers to systematically analyze vulnerabilities and develop universal defenses. Adversaries continuously exploit this opacity, crafting adaptive attacks that bypass existing filters. The dynamic nature of these threats necessitates a shift from reactive patching to proactive, mathematically grounded security guarantees, which currently remain elusive for complex neural architectures.

**Multi-modal Threats**

As the field transitions from text-only LLMs to Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), the attack surface expands exponentially. The integration of visual, auditory, and other sensory inputs introduces novel vectors for exploitation that are not present in unimodal systems. Recent research highlights the severe vulnerabilities inherent in these multi-modal architectures. For instance, MLLMs are highly susceptible to transferable adversarial examples, where perturbations in the visual input can manipulate the model's textual output. Existing methods often focus on aligning global features, such as CLIP's [CLS] token, but adversaries can exploit the rich local information encoded in patch tokens to achieve highly effective targeted attacks [Jia_2025_Adversarial].

Moreover, the alignment processes themselves, such as Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), which are crucial for steering text-to-image (T2I) models toward human preferences, introduce new vulnerabilities. Adversaries can execute clean-label poisoning attacks by exploiting vulnerabilities in multi-modal RLHF pipelines. By inducing visual feature collisions in reward models, attackers can corrupt the reward signals without altering the preference annotations, thereby hijacking the T2I generation process to produce harmful or targeted content [Duan_2025_RLHF]. These cross-modal interactions complicate the defense landscape, as sanitizing one modality (e.g., text) is insufficient if the malicious payload is embedded in another (e.g., an image). Addressing these multi-modal threats requires holistic defense strategies that analyze and sanitize inputs across all modalities simultaneously.

**Evaluation Bottlenecks**

A critical impediment to advancing LLM security is the lack of standardized, comprehensive evaluation frameworks. As the variety and sophistication of attacks proliferate, determining the comparative efficacy of different threats and defenses becomes increasingly difficult. Current evaluation mechanisms are often inadequate, relying on fragmented datasets and inconsistent metrics, which leaves LLMs vulnerable to threats like data exposure, misinformation, and the facilitation of illegal activities [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking].

The pertinent inquiry emerges: How can the research community reliably quantify and compare the effectiveness of attack 'A' versus attack 'B' through rational and reproducible observations? The establishment of a standardized benchmark for evaluating attacks and defenses on LLMs is urgently needed [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. Without unified metrics, researchers struggle to assess whether a proposed defense genuinely improves robustness or merely overfits to a specific attack dataset. Furthermore, evaluating the security of generative models is inherently challenging because the output space is vast and open-ended. Automated evaluation using LLMs as judges has gained traction, but this approach introduces its own biases and reliability issues. Overcoming these evaluation bottlenecks requires the development of dynamic, continuously updated benchmarks that accurately reflect the evolving threat landscape, alongside rigorous, multi-faceted metrics that capture both security and utility.

**Agentic Security**

The evolution of LLMs into autonomous agents capable of reasoning, planning, and interacting with external environments through tool use represents a significant leap in AI capabilities. However, this autonomy introduces profound security risks, collectively termed "Agentic Security." When LLM agents are granted access to external tools—such as web browsers, databases, or APIs—they become susceptible to indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks. In an IPI attack, malicious instructions are embedded within the external data retrieved by the agent (e.g., a compromised webpage), which the agent then inadvertently executes [Zhan_2025_LLM].

Despite the development of defenses designed to mitigate IPI attacks, their robustness remains highly questionable due to the complex and unpredictable nature of agent-environment interactions [Zhan_2025_LLM]. The strong planning capabilities of LLMs, which enable them to navigate complex environments, paradoxically make them more effective vehicles for executing sophisticated, multi-step exploits when compromised [Wang_2025_LLM]. Evaluating the security of these black-box agents is challenging, necessitating novel fuzzing frameworks that can systematically conduct IPI attacks across various architectures and tasks. Techniques combining high-quality prompt templates, adaptive seed scoring, and advanced search algorithms are required to uncover vulnerabilities in these complex systems [Wang_2025_LLM]. Securing LLM agents demands rigorous access controls, robust input validation at the tool interface, and the development of "least privilege" principles tailored for autonomous AI systems.

**Future Directions**

Addressing the myriad challenges in LLM security requires a concerted, multi-disciplinary effort. Future research must pivot towards several key directions to ensure the safe deployment of these powerful technologies.

First, the development of robust, modality-agnostic defense mechanisms is imperative. As multi-modal threats become more prevalent, defenses must evolve to detect and neutralize malicious payloads regardless of the input modality. This includes advancing techniques for cross-modal input sanitization and developing custom defense prompts that are resilient to complex jailbreak attempts [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking].

Second, the community must prioritize the creation of dynamic and standardized evaluation benchmarks. These benchmarks should not only measure the success rate of attacks and defenses but also quantify the associated alignment tax on model utility. Collaborative efforts to establish open-source, continuously updated leaderboards will foster transparency and accelerate progress.

Third, securing LLM agents requires foundational research into verifiable and constrained reasoning. Developing architectures where the agent's planning and execution phases are strictly decoupled and monitored can mitigate the risks of indirect prompt injections. Furthermore, integrating formal verification methods to mathematically prove the safety properties of certain model behaviors, while challenging, represents a crucial frontier.

Finally, proactive security measures, such as red-teaming and automated vulnerability discovery (e.g., fuzzing frameworks for agents), must be integrated into the entire lifecycle of model development, from pre-training to deployment. By anticipating threats and embedding security principles at the core of LLM architectures, the research community can pave the way for AI systems that are not only highly capable but also fundamentally secure and trustworthy.

conclusion.title: Conclusion
conclusion.text:
**Conclusion**

**Synthesis**
The rapid integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into diverse applications has undeniably transformed the landscape of artificial intelligence. However, as explored throughout this work, this proliferation has been accompanied by a complex and evolving array of security vulnerabilities. A comprehensive examination of the threat landscape reveals that LLMs are susceptible to a diverse range of attacks, including adversarial manipulations, data and model poisoning, and sophisticated jailbreaking techniques [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. Furthermore, the integration of external tools to create autonomous LLM agents has introduced new attack vectors, such as indirect prompt injection (IPI), which exploit the expanded attack surface [Zhan_2025_LLM]. Despite significant efforts to ensure model alignment and develop defensive mechanisms, many current safeguards remain inadequate. They often struggle to adapt to novel attack strategies, inadvertently degrade the model's performance on benign tasks, or present substantial barriers to scalable implementation [Zhang_2025_Real]. Consequently, understanding and countering these multifaceted threats remains a formidable challenge for the AI community.

**Practical Recommendations**
To mitigate these risks in the immediate term, organizations must adopt a multi-layered and proactive approach to LLM security. First and foremost, the implementation of robust, real-time monitoring systems is essential to effectively detect anomalies and malicious interactions, as current static evaluation mechanisms frequently fall short [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. Practitioners should exercise extreme caution when integrating LLMs with external tools, databases, or APIs, ensuring that strict input validation, sanitization, and access controls are in place to thwart indirect prompt injections [Zhan_2025_LLM]. Additionally, organizations must implement advanced security protocols tailored to the specific context of their applications, recognizing that a one-size-fits-all defense is insufficient against highly adaptable adversaries [Yang_2024_Adversarial]. Continuous red-teaming, adversarial training, and rigorous vulnerability assessments should become standard practice throughout the model lifecycle.

**Secure Deployment**
The imperative for secure deployment becomes particularly acute when LLMs are utilized in critical sectors, such as healthcare automation, legal analysis, or financial services. In these high-stakes environments, the consequences of a successful attack—ranging from sensitive data exposure and the generation of misinformation to the facilitation of malicious activities—can be devastating [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. Therefore, it is crucial to safeguard these technologies through rigorous alignment processes that prioritize information security and strict ethical constraints [Zhang_2025_Real]. Deploying custom or specialized LLMs requires implementing robust security safeguards that protect against both known vulnerabilities and emergent threats, ensuring their reliable, safe, and compliant use in sensitive applications [Yang_2024_Adversarial].

**Future Outlook**
Looking ahead, the pursuit of secure LLMs requires a concerted effort from the research community to develop more resilient and adaptive defensive strategies. Future research must focus on creating dynamic defenses that can evolve alongside emerging attack vectors without compromising the underlying utility and responsiveness of the models [Zhang_2025_Real]. Investigating the structural changes in models during attacks—such as the observation that the weights of models compromised via malicious fine-tuning exhibit larger norms—offers a promising avenue for developing novel, targeted mitigation strategies [Yang_2024_Adversarial]. Ultimately, enhancing the intrinsic robustness of LLMs, establishing standardized and comprehensive evaluation frameworks, and fostering transparency will be critical steps toward gaining and maintaining the trust of end-users [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. As LLMs continue to advance, prioritizing security as a fundamental design principle, rather than an afterthought, will be essential to realizing their full potential safely and responsibly.
